claims.text: Increasing oxygen-vacancy concentration in Co3O4-based catalysts enhances CO oxidation rates.
Oxygen vacancies provide additional active sites for CO adsorption and activation.
Co3O4 synthesized under stoichiometric oxidation conditions has minimal inherent oxygen vacancies.
Controlled thermal treatment in an inert gas such as N2 can increase and tune the oxygen-vacancy concentration in Co3O4.
The proposed CO oxidation comparison will be conducted at 200–300 °C under otherwise identical flow conditions.
XPS and Raman spectroscopy can characterize oxygen-vacancy concentration in these catalysts.
In situ DRIFTS can help confirm that vacancy concentration, rather than another structural feature, is the predominantly changed variable.
Vacancy-mediated CO adsorption and activation lowers the activation energy for CO oxidation.
Oxygen vacancies may alter selectivity by reducing overoxidation.
Dynamic redox cycling involving oxygen vacancies may affect catalyst durability.
Vacancy-rich Co3O4 catalysts are predicted to exhibit higher CO oxidation activity than nearly stoichiometric Co3O4.
Vacancy-rich catalysts are predicted to exhibit a shifted oxidation-product selectivity profile relative to the nearly stoichiometric baseline.
Excessively high oxygen-vacancy densities may destabilize and deactivate the catalyst.
The proposed vacancy–performance relationship is expected to hold at 200–300 °C and only for particular CO:O2 feed ratios.
Sintering or unintended electronic changes could confound attribution of performance changes to oxygen vacancies.
The relationship between oxygen-vacancy concentration and catalytic performance may be nonlinear.

The hypothesis would be falsified if increased vacancy concentration did not consistently enhance CO oxidation activity and alter selectivity relative to the baseline, or if observed performance changes instead tracked other structural modifications.
